meta.date: ~559–545 BC (engraved); the crisis under Ahaz ~734 BC

world_behind.title: Two small kings against one
world_behind.text: Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel allied and marched on Jerusalem to force Judah into their coalition, planning to replace Ahaz with a man of their choosing. The book of Kings records the same campaign and the same pair of attackers. This chapter is a prophet's intervention in a live military emergency.

world_behind.title: A king already decided
world_behind.text: Ahaz's answer to the crisis, recorded elsewhere, was to buy Assyria's protection with temple silver. Isaiah meets him before that decision is executed, and the whole exchange in verses 3 through 14 is an attempt to change a policy the king has effectively already chosen.

world_behind.title: The meeting place
world_behind.text: The prophet is sent to the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller's field. That is the city's water supply and its laundry ground. A king would be standing there if he were inspecting whether Jerusalem could survive a siege. Isaiah finds him doing exactly what a frightened ruler does.

world_behind.title: A son brought along
world_behind.text: Isaiah is told to bring Shearjashub, and the boy's name is not explained here. Later in this same block the words return as a promise about a remnant that returns, so the child standing beside the prophet is carrying a message his father does not have to say out loud.

world_behind.title: Butter and honey
world_behind.text: Verses 15 and 22 describe a diet of curds and honey, and the chapter frames it two ways. It is what a child of promise eats, and it is what is left to eat when the vineyards are gone and a household is down to one cow and two sheep. The same menu is a sign and a ration.

world_behind.title: A prophecy with a date on it
world_behind.text: Verse 8 attaches a number to the promise: within sixty-five years Ephraim will be broken past being a people. Most of Isaiah's timetables are vague on purpose, and this one is not. A hearer could write it on a wall and check it, which is a different kind of claim from the ones the block usually makes.

words.text: Bound by treaty. The news that reaches the house of David is that two neighbors have signed with each other. Isaiah's crisis begins with a diplomatic fact, and the word is precise about what frightened Jerusalem: an alliance.

A cloth worker who washed and thickened new wool, using water in quantity and space to spread the cloth. The fuller's field sat outside the wall near the water channel. Naming it puts the confrontation at an ordinary industrial site, and it means the prophet delivers a message about a virgin's son standing next to a laundry.

Sticks pulled from a fire, still smoking but no longer burning. Isaiah calls two kings the tails of these, the cold end of something already spent. It is a deliberately small word for a coalition that has terrified an entire capital, and the size of the insult is the argument.

Sixty, counted in twenties. The word appears once in this record and ninety-three times in the King James Bible, and its single appearance here sits inside quoted Isaiah: "within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken" (v. 8). The record's own narrators never reach for the idiom, so it marks the seam between copied text and Nephite prose as plainly as punctuation would.

cites.quote: within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken

spans.text: within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken

words.text: Silver pieces, an old English word for the coin. A thousand vines at a thousand silverlings is a premium vineyard, one coin per vine, and the verse's point is that the best land goes to briers along with the worst. The archaic term is kept in the record where a modern word would flatten it.

A hand tool for breaking ground, part pick and part hoe. The last verse is about hillsides too steep for the plow, worked by hand. It closes a chapter of national politics on a picture of small farming, and the promise there is modest: cattle will graze where vineyards used to be.

phrases.term: As the trees of the wood are moved with the wind
phrases.text: The whole royal house and the whole population, described as a stand of trees in a gust. Nothing in the image suggests damage. The trees are simply all leaning the same way at once, which is what panic looks like from outside, and it is the chapter's first hint that the danger to Judah is the fear of the two kings.

phrases.term: Take heed, and be quiet; fear not
phrases.text: The first thing the prophet says to a terrified king is an instruction to stop. Three imperatives arrive before any information about the outcome, and the middle one is the strangest thing to tell a man expecting a siege. Isaiah's counsel throughout this chapter is that the correct action is often the absence of an action.

phrases.term: If ye will not believe surely ye shall not be established
phrases.text: The chapter's hinge, and it is conditional in both directions. The verb behind establishing and the verb behind believing are close in the Hebrew, so the sentence reportedly turns on a single root: no holding firm without holding on. What survives in English is a plain warning that security is downstream of trust rather than of alliances.

phrases.term: Ask it either in the depths, or in the heights above
phrases.text: The King James offers a choice between "the depth" and "the height" (Isa. 7:11), singular. This reading makes both plural, widening the offer from two locations to two whole ranges. God is not proposing a menu of two signs; he is telling Ahaz that anything anywhere is available, which makes the refusal in the next verse harder to read as modesty.

phrases.term: A virgin shall conceive, and shall bear a son
phrases.text: The sign given after the sign was refused. Matthew quotes this verse at the birth of Christ and supplies the name's meaning, "they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us" (Matt. 1:23). Nephi's readers had already been shown the woman in vision, where an angel told his brother that "the virgin whom thou seest is the mother of the Son of God" (1 Ne. 11:18), so the record meets this verse with its identification already made.

phrases.term: The fly that is in the uttermost part of Egypt
phrases.text: The King James places the fly in "the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt" (Isa. 7:18). Dropping the rivers moves the summons from the delta to the country as a whole, and it pairs more evenly with the bee in the land of Assyria in the same verse. Two empires are whistled for like insects. This is the second time in three chapters that God signals for a nation the way a keeper signals for a swarm.

phrases.term: Shave with a razor that is hired
phrases.text: Assyria is the razor, and the razor is rented. Ahaz was on the point of paying Assyria to save him, so the metaphor tells him what his money will actually purchase: the head, the hair of the feet, and the beard. That is total humiliation, described from top to bottom. The prophecy does not forbid the alliance. It prices it.

verses.label: v. 1–8
verses.title: The variants here mostly take words away
verses.text: Thirteen of these twenty-five verses differ from Isaiah 7, and the profile is the reverse of the neighbouring chapters: eleven deletions against two insertions. Verses 1 and 8 are typical, each losing a single small word and nothing else. Where 2 Nephi 12 widens by adding clauses, the revision here works by removing connective ones.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: The sign is offered in two directions, both made plural
verses.text: Isaiah has "ask it either in the depth, or in the height above." Here both nouns become plural, depths and heights. The offer is unchanged in substance and enlarged in scale, and these are the only two words in the verse the variants touch.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: One auxiliary is added to the sign itself
verses.text: The verse that gives the sign of the virgin gains a shall. It is a single word in the chapter's most quoted line, and it is one of only two insertions anywhere in the twenty-five verses.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: Egypt entire, instead of its waterways
verses.text: Isaiah hisses for the fly "in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt." The variants drop the rivers of. A geographic detail disappears and the summons widens from a delta to a country.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: The razor loses its explanatory word
verses.text: Isaiah's verse names the hired razor "namely, by them beyond the river." Namely is cut here. The apposition still stands, and the text no longer pauses to mark it as an explanation. That is the same economy the deletions apply throughout the chapter.

chapter.title: A sermon delivered inside an emergency
chapter.text: Nothing here is theoretical. Verse 1 names four kings across three generations, Ahaz son of Jotham son of Uzziah, plus Rezin and Pekah; verse 3 names the meeting place to the yard, "the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field"; and verse 8 puts a term on the outcome, "within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken." A doctrine of trust is offered as the alternative to a treaty, and verse 12 records the refusal in the king's own words, "I will not ask, neither will I tempt the Lord."

chapter.title: The most quoted verse in the chapter answers a refusal
chapter.text: The Immanuel sign is not given to a believing king in a moment of worship. It is given to a man who has just declined to ask for anything, and it is addressed to the house of David rather than to him. The most famous promise in Isaiah arrives as a rebuke.

chapter.title: Belief is what holds the building up
chapter.text: Verse 9 makes establishment conditional on believing, and the rest of the chapter shows a king who chose to be established by other means and got shaved by them. The argument is that nothing else holds.

chapter.title: The chapter's images shrink as its stakes grow
chapter.text: Four reductions run through the chapter in order. Two kings become "the two tails of these smoking firebrands" at verse 4. Two empires become "the fly that is in the uttermost part of Egypt" and "the bee that is in the land of Assyria" at verse 18. An imperial invasion becomes "a razor that is hired" at verse 20. National ruin becomes "a young cow and two sheep" at verse 21. The events grow larger at each step and the images grow smaller, and verse 23 gives the scale that was lost, "a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings."

chapter.title: Why Nephi copied it
chapter.text: A small people facing larger neighbors and asked to trust is the colony's situation as much as Judah's. The chapter also carries verse 14, "a virgin shall conceive, and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel," which 1 Nephi 11:13–20 reports the copyist having seen in vision. Politics and Messiah stand in one chapter, which is what 2 Nephi 25:1–5 says the manner of the Jews does and what 2 Nephi 11:2 gives as the reason for copying thirteen of these chapters.

chapter.title: The sign is both near and far
chapter.text: A child born in Ahaz's lifetime marks the timetable in verses 15 and 16, and the same words are read by Matthew as a prophecy of Christ. The chapter does not resolve the two, and the record does not resolve them either. Both readings are left standing in the text as Nephi copied it.

applications.title: Notice which verse describes your problem
applications.text: The military facts got one sentence and the fear got a longer one. Write out a current difficulty twice, once as events and once as your reaction, and see which paragraph is doing more damage.

applications.title: Try being quiet as an action
applications.text: Isaiah's first counsel to a king under threat was to stop moving. Identify one situation where you have been generating activity out of anxiety, and deliberately do nothing about it for a set period, then reassess.

applications.title: Ask for the sign
applications.text: Ahaz refused an offer that was genuinely open, using reverent language to protect a decision he had already made. Where have you declined to seek an answer because you suspect it would require changing course? Ask this week.

applications.title: Price the alliance
applications.text: Before buying security, name what the purchase costs beyond money: dependence, obligation, exposure. The razor in this chapter was hired, and the payment did not prevent the shave.

applications.title: Put a name on the promise
applications.text: The sign's content is a name meaning God with us. Say, in a single line, where God has actually been with you in the last month, and be specific enough that the sentence could not be said by anyone else.

applications.title: Check what you are established on
applications.text: List the three things that make you feel secure. Then ask, honestly, which of them would survive a bad year, and whether belief is anywhere on the list.

questions.text: When was the last time my heart moved like trees in the wind, and what was actually at risk?
What would "be quiet" mean this week in the situation I am most anxious about?
If believing and being established are the same act, what am I currently standing on?
Have I ever used reverent language to avoid an answer I did not want?
What difference would it make to me today if the name Immanuel were literally true of my situation?
What have I hired to protect me that could turn on me?
